items.stem: Distinguish between signing a treaty and ratifying a treaty.
items.answer: Signing shows intention to be bound and an obligation not to defeat the treaty's purpose; ratifying is the formal consent to be legally bound, usually after domestic approval (e.g. US Senate consent).
items.markingKey: Signing shows intention to be bound and an obligation not to defeat the treaty's purpose; ratifying is the formal consent to be legally bound, usually after domestic approval (e.g. US Senate consent). items.stem: Using the CRC and child labour as an example, explain limits of treaty implementation.
items.answer: The CRC (Art. 32) protects children from economic exploitation; the ILO estimated 160 million children were in child labour in 2020. near-universal ratification has not ended child labour, showing that poverty and weak enforcement limit treaty impact

items.answer: The UN Human Rights Committee found that Tasmanian laws criminalising sex between men violated the right to privacy under the ICCPR; Tasmania repealed the laws in 1997. an individual complaint led to a finding that prompted domestic legal change, despite non-binding status

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that international human rights treaties have little effect on how states behave.
items.answer: Treaties rarely change behaviour on their own, but they give domestic actors tools to press for change, especially in democracies.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: ratification without implementation (Afghanistan, child labour); no enforcement; reservations. Arguments against: legal change after treaty body findings (Toonen); domestic courts apply treaties; civil society uses treaties (Simmons, Mobilizing for Human Rights). Supported judgement: Treaties rarely change behaviour on their own, but they give domestic actors tools to press for change, especially in democracies.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that the refusal of the United States to ratify key treaties undermines the international human rights system?
items.answer: US non-ratification weakens the system's legitimacy and US credibility, but the system's survival depends far more on broader state practice.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: sets precedent of selectivity; weakens US criticism of others. Arguments against: US protects many rights domestically; system has near-universal participation without the US; others also violate treaties they ratified. Supported judgement: US non-ratification weakens the system's legitimacy and US credibility, but the system's survival depends far more on broader state practice. items.stem: Briefly explain why the ICC has been accused of bias against Africa.
items.answer: Most of its early cases and convictions concerned African defendants (e.g. DRC, Uganda, Sudan, Kenya), while powerful non-members (US, China, Russia) were beyond reach; several cases were Security Council or self-referrals. Recent investigations (Ukraine, Palestine, Philippines, Venezuela, Afghanistan) have broadened its geographic focus.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the Universal Periodic Review and treaty body review.
items.answer: The UPR is a peer review by states of all UN members' human rights records, regardless of treaty membership; treaty body review is conducted by independent experts and applies only to states that have ratified that treaty.

items.stem: "The Human Rights Council is a court that can punish states." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The Council is a political body of states; it can adopt resolutions, create commissions of inquiry and appoint rapporteurs, but it cannot issue binding judgments or penalties.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "ICCPR"?
options: The principle that the ICC acts only when national courts are unwilling or unable genuinely to investigate or prosecute
The space of voluntary associations, NGOs, movements and media between the state, the market and the family
The court in Strasbourg that enforces the European Convention on Human Rights for the 46 member states of the Council of Europe
The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966, in force 1976), monitored by the Human Rights Committee
items.answer: The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966, in force 1976), monitored by the Human Rights Committee
items.markingKey: D. "ICCPR" is the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966, in force 1976), monitored by the Human Rights Committee.

items.stem: Which of the following former heads of state was arrested in March 2025 and transferred to the ICC in The Hague?
items.answer: Rodrigo Duterte of the Philippines
items.markingKey: D. He faces charges of crimes against humanity linked to his "war on drugs".

items.stem: Which of the following NGOs was founded in 1961 after Peter Benenson's article "The Forgotten Prisoners"?
items.answer: Amnesty International
items.markingKey: C. Amnesty won the 1977 Nobel Peace Prize.

items.stem: Diego writes: "The Responsibility to Protect is a binding treaty obligation." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: R2P is a political commitment from the 2005 World Summit Outcome Document, not a treaty; it builds on existing law such as the Genocide Convention.
items.markingKey: R2P is a political commitment from the 2005 World Summit Outcome Document, not a treaty; it builds on existing law such as the Genocide Convention. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the ICESCR and the ICCPR.
items.answer: The ICCPR covers civil and political rights requiring immediate respect (e.g. no torture, free expression); the ICESCR covers economic, social and cultural rights (work, health, education) realised progressively.
items.markingKey: The ICCPR covers civil and political rights requiring immediate respect (e.g. no torture, free expression); the ICESCR covers economic, social and cultural rights (work, health, education) realised progressively. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the Human Rights Council replaced the Commission on Human Rights.
items.answer: The Commission was discredited because states with poor records joined it to shield themselves and others; the Council introduced the Universal Periodic Review, competitive election by the General Assembly and the possibility of suspending members (Libya 2011, Russia 2022).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The Commission was discredited because states with poor records joined it to shield themselves and others; the Council introduced the Universal Periodic Review, competitive election by the General Assembly and the possibility of suspending members (Libya 2011, Russia 2022). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a state report to a treaty body and an NGO shadow report.
items.answer: A state report presents the government's account of implementation; an NGO shadow report gives civil society's independent assessment, often highlighting gaps the state omits.
items.markingKey: A state report presents the government's account of implementation; an NGO shadow report gives civil society's independent assessment, often highlighting gaps the state omits. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why R2P was designed to work through the UN Security Council.
items.answer: To gain wide acceptance in 2005, states limited collective action to Security Council authorisation under Chapter VII, reassuring those who feared unilateral intervention by powerful states, though this also means the veto can block action.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: To gain wide acceptance in 2005, states limited collective action to Security Council authorisation under Chapter VII, reassuring those who feared unilateral intervention by powerful states, though this also means the veto can block action. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that once a state ratifies CEDAW, discrimination against women in that state ends. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Ratification creates legal obligations and reporting duties, but discrimination often persists; implementation depends on domestic law and practice, and the CEDAW Committee can only make recommendations.
items.markingKey: Ratification creates legal obligations and reporting duties, but discrimination often persists; implementation depends on domestic law and practice, and the CEDAW Committee can only make recommendations. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using the ICC arrest warrants for Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant (November 2024) as an example, explain the politics of international criminal justice.
items.answer: The ICC issued warrants for the Israeli prime minister and former defence minister for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza; the US imposed sanctions on ICC officials in 2025. the case shows the ICC acting against leaders allied with powerful states, and the political backlash that limits enforcement

items.stem: Using Amnesty International's 2022 apartheid report on Israel as an example, explain contested NGO legitimacy.
items.answer: Amnesty concluded that Israel maintained a system of apartheid against Palestinians; Israel and several governments rejected the report, while others cited it. the report demonstrated NGO agenda-setting power but also how NGOs' legitimacy is contested in politicised conflicts
items.markingKey: Context (Amnesty concluded that Israel maintained a system of apartheid against Palestinians; Israel and several governments rejected the report, while others cited it.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Sovereignty no longer exclusively protects states from foreign interference; it is a charge of responsibility that holds states accountable for the welfare of their people."
— Paraphrase of the ICISS report The Responsibility to Protect, 2001

Explain, with reference to the source, the idea of sovereignty as responsibility.
items.answer: Sovereignty is redefined from a shield against interference to a duty to protect people; if a state fails, its claim to non-interference weakens.
items.markingKey: Sovereignty is redefined from a shield against interference to a duty to protect people; if a state fails, its claim to non-interference weakens. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: A student claims that the Human Rights Committee and the Human Rights Council are the same body. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The Human Rights Committee is an expert treaty body monitoring the ICCPR; the Human Rights Council is an intergovernmental body of 47 states created in 2006.
items.markingKey: The Human Rights Committee is an expert treaty body monitoring the ICCPR; the Human Rights Council is an intergovernmental body of 47 states created in 2006. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Justice that depends on the cooperation of the very states whose leaders are accused is justice that waits a very long time."
— Commentary on international criminal justice, 2024 (adapted)

With reference to the source, explain one weakness of the ICC.
items.answer: The ICC has no police force and relies on states to arrest and surrender suspects; when states protect accused leaders (e.g. Putin, al-Bashir), cases stall.

items.stem: A student claims that the Responsibility to Protect means the international community must use military force whenever human rights are violated. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: R2P covers only four mass atrocity crimes and emphasises prevention, assistance and peaceful measures; force is a last resort that requires Security Council authorisation.
items.markingKey: R2P covers only four mass atrocity crimes and emphasises prevention, assistance and peaceful measures; force is a last resort that requires Security Council authorisation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "International human rights treaties have little effect on how states behave."
items.answer: Treaties rarely change behaviour on their own, but they give domestic actors tools to press for change, especially in democracies.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: ratification without implementation (Afghanistan, child labour); no enforcement; reservations. Arguments against: legal change after treaty body findings (Toonen); domestic courts apply treaties; civil society uses treaties (Simmons, Mobilizing for Human Rights). Supported judgement: Treaties rarely change behaviour on their own, but they give domestic actors tools to press for change, especially in democracies.

items.stem: "Regional human rights courts protect rights more effectively than UN mechanisms." Discuss.
items.answer: Regional courts are generally more effective where they exist, but coverage is uneven and they depend on state goodwill.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: binding judgments (ECtHR, IACtHR); higher compliance in Europe. Arguments against: regional systems absent in Asia; non-compliance (Russia, Türkiye, UK on prisoner voting); UN mechanisms are universal. Supported judgement: Regional courts are generally more effective where they exist, but coverage is uneven and they depend on state goodwill. items.stem: To what extent is it true that naming and shaming changes the behaviour of human rights violators?
items.answer: Naming and shaming works best when targets value their reputation or depend on outside support; it is weakest against powerful or isolated regimes.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: reputational costs and aid conditions; release of prisoners after campaigns. Arguments against: powerful states ignore criticism (China on Xinjiang); can provoke backlash or more repression. Supported judgement: Naming and shaming works best when targets value their reputation or depend on outside support; it is weakest against powerful or isolated regimes. items.stem: With reference to two specific examples you have studied, evaluate the argument that the Responsibility to Protect is a tool used by powerful states to justify intervention in weaker states.
items.answer: R2P can be misused, but its design actually limits unilateralism; selectivity reflects great-power politics more than the norm itself.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Libya regime change; selective application. Arguments against: R2P restricts unilateral intervention by requiring SC approval; African Union supported similar principles; prevention focus.
